Institutional policy

sec.p: The dynamic nature of the framework becomes evident where these stages interact. If monitoring reveals that the predictive system produces inaccurate or disproportionately adverse outcomes for particular student groups, this would generate a new governance concern under Pillar II and require the institution to reconsider the system’s design or use under Pillar I and strengthen its oversight and accountability mechanisms under Pillar III. The feedback process therefore allows governance measures to evolve alongside the technology and the risks identified during its operation. This example is hypothetical. It is intended to show how the framework could be used and the framework has not yet been tested in an actual institutional setting.

The framework is designed to be sufficiently flexible to operate across diverse regulatory environments. While particularly informed by the GDPR and the European Union AI Act 2024, its principles remain applicable to jurisdictions where AI-specific regulation is still emerging, including Kuwait and other countries. In such contexts, the framework may serve as a reference model for the development of institutional AI governance policies and practices.

sec.title: 8. Discussion
sec.p: The findings of this study highlight the growing complexity of AI governance within higher education and demonstrate that effective governance requires a balance between technological innovation, data protection, ethical responsibility and institutional accountability. By integrating insights from the literature review, regulatory analysis and the proposed conceptual framework, several important observations emerge.

First, the findings reinforce the central importance of data privacy within AI governance while demonstrating that privacy-related risks extend beyond traditional concerns regarding data collection and storage. The analysis reveals that re-identification risks, inadequate consent mechanisms, third-party vendor dependence and cybersecurity vulnerabilities represent interconnected dimensions of a broader governance challenge. This finding supports Information Privacy Theory, which conceptualizes privacy not merely as the protection of information but as the preservation of individual control over how personal data is collected, processed and utilized. Consequently, governance strategies that rely solely on compliance-oriented data protection measures are unlikely to provide sufficient protection unless accompanied by broader institutional mechanisms promoting transparency, accountability and stakeholder trust.

Second, the findings demonstrate the increasingly significant influence of regulatory frameworks on institutional AI governance. The combined effect of the GDPR and the EU AI Act 2024 reflects a broader shift towards risk-based governance models that seek to balance innovation with the protection of fundamental rights. However, the analysis suggests that compliance alone is insufficient to ensure responsible AI adoption. Institutions must also develop internal governance capabilities capable of anticipating emerging risks, monitoring evolving technologies and responding to stakeholder concerns. This observation aligns with Institutional Theory, which suggests that sustainable organizational change is shaped not only by external regulatory pressures but also by the internalization of professional norms and governance expectations.

Existing research has proposed several approaches to AI governance in higher education. Chan (2023)’s AI Ecological Education Policy Framework organizes institutional AI policy around three dimensions: pedagogical, governance and operational dimensions. Similarly, Shahid et al. (2026) propose a multi-dimensional framework for generative AI in higher education, emphasizing responsible use of large language models, academic integrity, AI literacy, institutional accountability and alignment with national AI policy. More recently, Khoza et al. (2026) identify growing convergence among university AI-governance approaches around principles such as transparency, fairness and accountability, while also highlighting a movement towards more proactive and adaptable governance.

The framework proposed in this study complements these approaches but differs in its analytical structure and regulatory emphasis. Rather than organizing governance primarily around institutional functions or specific forms of generative AI, it explicitly connects three elements: the technologies and benefits driving AI adoption, the governance risks arising from that adoption, and the legal and institutional mechanisms available to address those risks. It also integrates the GDPR and EU AI Act as comparative regulatory benchmarks, thereby linking higher-education governance concerns with more specific requirements concerning data protection, risk management, transparency and human oversight.

The framework further treats these elements as interdependent rather than static categories. As illustrated in Section 7.3, the identification of new risks may require changes to both the way an AI system is deployed and the governance mechanisms surrounding it. The contribution of the framework therefore lies not in replacing existing higher-education AI-governance models, but in providing a complementary structure that connects innovation, higher-education-specific governance risks and regulatory responses through an iterative process.

The findings also highlight the growing importance of third-party vendor governance. As universities increasingly rely on external AI providers, institutional control over data processing activities becomes more fragmented and difficult to monitor. Many governance risks originate not from institutional misuse of AI but from insufficient oversight of external technology providers and the complex cross-border data ecosystems in which these providers operate. Consequently, institutions should strengthen vendor governance through robust procurement procedures, contractual safeguards, data processing agreements and ongoing monitoring mechanisms. Such measures are particularly important where AI services involve the transfer or processing of sensitive educational data across multiple jurisdictions.

The Kuwaiti context illustrates both the opportunities and challenges associated with AI adoption in environments where AI-specific regulation remains underdeveloped. While higher education institutions are increasingly embracing AI technologies to support teaching, learning, research and administration, governance structures have not always evolved at the same pace. This creates the possibility that technological adoption may outstrip institutional governance capacity, increasing exposure to privacy, security and accountability risks. At the same time, the relative absence of comprehensive domestic AI regulation creates an opportunity for institutions to adopt proactive governance practices informed by international standards and emerging best practices. From an Institutional Theory perspective, this reflects the importance of normative governance mechanisms in shaping responsible organisational behaviour in the absence of strong coercive regulatory pressures.

The findings suggest that the long-term success of AI adoption in higher education will depend not only on technological capability but also on the development of governance frameworks capable of fostering transparency, accountability, privacy protection, security and stakeholder trust. Universities should therefore move beyond reactive compliance approaches and adopt integrated governance strategies that embed ethical considerations, risk management and regulatory awareness throughout the AI lifecycle. The proposed framework contributes to this objective by providing a structured approach through which institutions can balance innovation with responsible governance and thereby support the sustainable integration of AI within higher education.

While the proposed framework provides a theoretically grounded approach to AI governance in higher education, it has not yet been empirically validated. Future research should examine its application across different institutional and regulatory contexts, particularly within emerging AI governance environments such as Kuwait.

sec.title: 9. Conclusion
sec.p: The rapid integration of AI into higher education has created significant opportunities for enhancing teaching, learning, research and institutional administration. At the same time, it has introduced complex challenges relating to data privacy, cybersecurity, algorithmic bias, transparency, accountability and regulatory compliance. As universities increasingly adopt AI-enabled systems, the development of effective governance mechanisms has become a strategic necessity rather than a purely technical or legal concern.

This paper examined the governance implications of AI adoption in higher education through a review of the literature, an analysis of the GDPR and the European Union AI Act 2024 and the application of Responsible Innovation Theory, Information Privacy Theory and Institutional Theory. The findings identified seven interconnected categories of governance challenges: data privacy and re-identification risks, third-party vendor dependence, misinformation and data integrity concerns, cybersecurity vulnerabilities, algorithmic bias, inadequate consent mechanisms, and governance, accountability and regulatory uncertainty. These challenges demonstrate that AI governance extends beyond regulatory compliance and requires a broader institutional approach that integrates ethical, technical, organisational and legal considerations.

To address this challenge, the study proposed a three-pillar conceptual framework integrating AI innovation, governance challenges and governance and compliance mechanisms. The framework contributes to the existing literature by providing a structured approach through which institutions can evaluate AI adoption holistically, balancing innovation objectives with the requirements of privacy protection, accountability, transparency and stakeholder trust. By linking technological opportunities with governance responsibilities, the framework seeks to move beyond the traditional view that governance constrains innovation and instead positions governance as a key enabler of sustainable and trustworthy AI adoption.

The significance of this contribution extends beyond the European regulatory environment. While the framework is informed by the GDPR and the EU AI Act 2024, its underlying principles are equally relevant to jurisdictions where AI governance frameworks remain under development. In Kuwait, where higher education institutions are increasingly embracing AI technologies as part of broader digital transformation strategies, the framework offers a practical reference point for strengthening governance capacity and supporting responsible innovation. The framework remains conceptual, and its practical value has yet to be established through empirical research. Case studies in Kuwaiti universities could help assess how well it works in practice.

The long-term success of AI in higher education will depend not solely on technological advancement but on the ability of institutions to govern these technologies responsibly. Universities that embed transparency, accountability, privacy protection and ethical oversight into their AI strategies will be better positioned to realise the benefits of AI while maintaining the trust of students, staff, regulators and society. As AI continues to reshape higher education, governance should not be viewed as a response to innovation but as an essential condition for its sustainable and responsible development.
